title: Booze and the news; Bright young journalists drank to death
article: When former Toronto Star police reporter John Duncanson died in his sleep back in January, his "once-brilliant career" cut short at 43, the obit writer described him as someone who stood out -- "even in the country's largest newsroom" -- and as a journalist who was "fearless, gritty and hungry to break important stories."
But, sadly, he was also a hopeless alcoholic and, despite a long struggle to fight its relentless grip, it was the alcoholic in John Duncanson that ultimately took him down.
It cost him his job, and then it cost him his life.

As any 12-stepper knows, however, ol' John Barleycorn can take down anyone, including a goodly number of old-school journalists in ages past and present -- although whisky in the top drawer and cigarette burns on the shirt are less a caricatured image in the newsrooms of today.
Over in the town of Port Hope, young Darryl Thompson was no John Duncanson.
He had never won a National Newspaper Award, let alone two, and nor had he ever won a Governor General's Award for public service journalism.

But he wasn't a bad sports reporter, the Cobourg Daily Star and the associated Port Hope Evening Guide being his last place of employ -- before he got caught stealing a bottle of booze from a local tavern, that is.
As editorial director Mandy Martin described him: "He was the best writer I had on staff at that time -- but (a person) with issues he either failed to address, or would not address."
Like alcoholism, for example.
And, later, his co-dependency on drugs -- a cross addiction that doubles the trouble, and adds grease to the already slippery slope.
It cost him his common-law marriage, a disconnect from his young daughter, a job which had been his passion and, finally, like John Duncanson, it cost him his life.

In all the years Ron Hoath has been the police chief of Port Hope, and he has been at the helm of the 25-officer force for more than two decades, he had never had an in\-custody death until Darryl Thompson ended up in one of his cells for public intoxication.
The next morning, instead of having slept it off, Thompson was found with nary a vital sign to his name.
At 36, all had come to an end.

Last week, Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU), which is mandated by the province to investigate all in\-custody deaths, cleared the Port Hope police service of any wrongdoing in Thompson's demise -- the toxicology results, as expected, being the true tale of the tape.

Shortly after Thompson's death, and therefore back in the early days of the SIU's investigation, it was written here that toxicology would likely reveal that the pain-killing opiate Oxycontin had probably played a major role and that, along with the booze, this deadly tag-team combination would be ruled the cause of Thompson's early exit.

Friends interviewed at the time, in fact, confirmed his addiction to that narcotic -- first legally prescribed to him when he lost a fingertip in a picture-framing factory -- and later hustled on the street when the scripts ran out.

But there were also whispers that he had been in contact with a certain street dealer earlier in the day in a hunt for liquid morphine, rumours that could not be confirmed and could therefore not be reported as fact.
Nor could the dealer be found.

With the release of the SIU's report, however, it can now be confirmed that those rumours were true and, when the mandatory inquest is finally held, no doubt more details will be flushed out, with the inadequacies of Port Hope's jail cells being another one of the focal points.
But one thing is certain.
With liquid morphine, Thompson had upped the ante on his addiction.
As the SIU's report stated, a post mortem was conducted and the cause of death was determined to be "intoxication with ethanol and hydromorphone."
In other words, booze and a narcotic chemical commonly referred to as liquid morphine were the killers.

According to medical experts, the adverse effects of hydromorphone are similar to those of other opioid analgesics, such as true morphine -- the major hazard being respiratory depression and cessation brought about by misuse, and all of which can be exaggerated further by "dose dumping" the medication with alcohol.
And Darryl Thompson has dose dumped.
There is no Cobourg Daily Star today, and no Port Hope Evening Guide.
They were recently melded into Northumberland Today.

When the SIU's findings were published, however, no mention was made in Northumberland Today of Thompson's former affiliation with those newspapers, and how he had been their sports writer up until 2006 when he was caught on video heisting a bottle of liquor from the old Shoeless Joe's in Cobourg.

There was a quote from Thompson's former spouse, however, in which she lays blame on no one but Thompson himself for his death in a drunk tank -- admitting that they separated in 2005 because of his use of drugs and alcohol.
If anything, she hoped the case of Darryl Thompson, once an outstanding sports writer, would become a "reality check for those who think drugs won't hurt them."
If only it were so.
